title: Streaming Responses
subtitle: assemble the pieces, survive the cut

beats.narration: Waiting for a complete response is fine, until the response is long and a user is staring at a blank screen. Streaming sends the response in pieces, as the model generates them. Feels faster. But it hands your code two new jobs: you assemble the final message yourself, and you decide what happens when the pieces stop coming early.

A streamed response is a series of events describing the message as it's being built. Message start opens the shell. Content block start opens a block at an index: text, tool use, or thinking. Content block delta appends fragments to it. Content block stop closes that block. Message delta carries the stop reason, and message stop says: the message is whole. Your handler applies each event to the partial state it's building. The end result is identical to a non-streamed response. The difference is that you assembled it, event by event.

elements.text:
same final message —
but YOU built it

beats.narration: Now the rule that keeps state clean: never act on a partial block. The dangerous one is tool use. Its input arrives as a partial JSON string, spread across many deltas. Until the block stop event, that string is not valid JSON. Parse it early and you choke, or worse, you run a tool with half its arguments. So collect deltas, act after the block closes. Same discipline one level up: append the assistant turn to history only after message stop, with every block fully assembled.

elements.text: Never act on a partial block

deltas:  {"account_i   ← not JSON yet!
         {"account_id": "A-44   ← still not!
stop →   {"account_id": "A-4471"}  ✓ parse now

beats.narration: Here's the postmortem that makes it real. An agent streamed responses so operators could watch. The handler collected deltas, and appended the turn to history when its read loop ended. In testing, on a fast local network, every stream ran to completion, so that worked every time. Then production. A network blip killed one stream after a tool use block had opened, but before it closed. The read loop ended, like always. The handler appended, like always. Except now history contained a tool call with truncated JSON inside. The operator retried, the retry carried the corrupted turn, and the API rejected it, pointing at the retry. The team spent an afternoon debugging schemas and retry logic. The bug was upstream: the loop ending and the message completing are not the same thing.

items.text: handler appends when read loop ends
append runs anyway → truncated JSON in history
retry carries the corrupted turn → rejected

elements.text:
error points at the retry —

beats.narration: So the survival rules. Gate the history append on message stop, explicitly. When a stream is interrupted, throw the partial turn away and retry from the last complete turn. Check the stop reason before continuing any loop: tool use means your calls are ready to run, anything else is a different path. And when a tool-use error shows up on a retry, ask whether the previous turn came from a stream, before you touch the schema.

items.text: interrupted? discard partial + retry from last complete turn
check stop_reason before continuing the loop
error on retry? suspect the stream first, schema second

beats.narration: Streaming buys responsiveness, and the price is assembly discipline: whole blocks, whole messages, nothing partial in history. Checkpoint four hands you a stream handler with exactly this bug. Repair it, then watch the walkthrough.
